steps.text: This line stores the text Alex under the name researcher. The quotation marks tell Python that Alex is text, rather than another variable to look up.
Here we store our research question as text. Nothing appears on screen yet; this line gives the question a name so we can use it later.
Print displays a greeting followed by the value stored in researcher. Python adds a space between these two items, so the output is Hello, Alex.
This line displays the question we stored earlier: How often did the shot go in? It appears on a new line, after the greeting.
This line assigns the number three to goals. The equals sign stores a value; it does not ask whether two values are equal.
This line stores five under the name shots. Goals and shots are separate variables, so setting shots does not change the value of goals.
Print looks up the current value of goals and displays three. If you change the first line to four and run again, this output becomes four.
The quotation marks make three and two text strings. Plus joins those strings, so print displays the characters three then two: 32. Without quotes, addition would produce five.
We begin by storing three goals. This is one input to our calculation, and changing it lets us test a different practice result.
We store five shot attempts. This total includes both goals and misses; dividing by attempts lets us compare results from different numbers of shots.
Divide three goals by five shots, then multiply by one hundred to get a percentage. Python stores sixty point zero in the variable named success rate.
This line prints the label Goals followed by three. A label makes the output easier to interpret than showing an unexplained number by itself.
This line prints Success rate followed by sixty point zero and a percent sign. It displays the value already calculated; it does not perform the division again.
This list stores five attempts in order. One means a goal and zero means a miss, so the list preserves more detail than a single total.
Sum adds the list entries, and print displays three. This counts goals because every goal contributes one and every miss contributes zero.
Len counts how many entries the list contains, so print displays five. Misses still count as attempts, even though their stored value is zero.
This comment explains our data: the practice records are invented, one means goal, and zero means miss. Python skips comments, but readers need this context.
We store five attempts as a list containing three ones and two zeros. Adding another goal means appending a new one, which also increases the attempt count.
Sum adds all the entries and stores three in goals. Using the list means the total will update automatically when we change the data and run again.
Len counts the entries and stores five in attempts. This counts every shot, including misses, so our percentage uses the full number of opportunities.
This line displays Goals followed by three. Check that this agrees with the number of ones in the list before trusting the final percentage.
This line displays Attempts followed by five. After appending another goal, it should display six; the extra goal is also an extra attempt.
This prints the success rate: three divided by five times one hundred, or sixty percent. Appending a goal gives four out of six, about sixty-seven percent.
This line creates a variable named goals, ending with an s, and stores three. Remember that exact name when you inspect the calculation below.
This line creates shots and stores five. Both intended inputs now exist, so our next check is whether the calculation uses their names consistently.
This comment gives us a debugging task. Python ignores the comment; we should compare the variable names already defined with the names used on the next line.
This line asks for goal without the final s. That name is undefined in this program, so Python raises a NameError before print can display a percentage.
This comment identifies our records as synthetic practice data. We can use them to check code, but they are not evidence about an actual player.
We save the research question as text. Writing the question explicitly helps another reader understand what the calculation is intended to describe.
This list records five invented attempts, with one for a goal and zero for a miss. Keep that meaning consistent when replacing the example data.
Print displays our question before the results: How often did each practice shot go in? This connects the following numbers to the purpose of our experiment.
Sum counts three goals from the list, and print displays that count beside the Goals label. The result comes from the current data, rather than a separate handwritten total.
Len counts all five attempts, and print displays the total beside Attempts. A reader needs this sample size to understand how much evidence the rate summarizes.
This divides three goals by five attempts and multiplies by one hundred, printing sixty percent. It describes this sample; it does not establish a player’s general skill.
The final line prints a limitation: this is a tiny synthetic sample. Keeping that statement beside the results helps prevent a correct calculation from becoming an unsupported claim.
